newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon scraps proposal to cut Army divisions.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon scraps proposal to cut Army divisions.

text.p: The Defense Department said on Thursday it had rejected the possibility of eliminating two of the Army's 10 combat divisions as part of a major review of U.S. military strategy and forces.

"That possibility is off the table," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said in response to questions on the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR), which will be sent to Congress on May 15 by Defense Secretary William Cohen.

Published reports have said officials involved in preparing the "QDR" were looking at a proposal to get rid of 50,000 or more of the Army's 495,000 active duty troops to save money for weapons modernization.
But Bacon, asked about the possibility of cutting two divisions -- which would include some 50,000 combat and support soldiers -- told reporters that plan had been scrapped.
He refused to say how many personnel could be cut from the current 1.4 million-member U.S. armed forces or whether the cuts might be charactized as "significant".
"I've given you a peek of what's not under the (Christmas) tree," Bacon said.
"The final decisions have not been made. I suppose that 'significant' is a term that people define in different ways. I think you should wait and see."
Army officials told Reuters after the announcement that senior officers in the service had fought the deep cut, calling the proposal "devastating" in the wake of Army cuts over the last five years.

Cohen had been reluctant to predict what the report would include, but has told reporters that the United States will concentrate on costly weapons modernization and would keep a forward presence of 100,000 troops in the western Pacific and 100,000 in Europe.
He said on Tuesday that the U.S. military still had far too many bases after the Cold War and he expected to decide quickly whether to press Congress for painful new closings.

The Pentagon has shut down dozens of big bases and hundreds of small facilities at home and abroad in recent years. But Cohen said more base reductions were needed to match post-Cold War troop cuts, which have already reduced U.S. troop strength to 1.4 million.

At stake in the QDR are arms including billions of dollars in new fighter jets planned by big defense contractors and possibly tens of thousands of civilian jobs at and around bases that might be closed.

A major stake in the deliberations includes whether the Pentagon will buy as many as 4,400 new attack jets in three planned programs at a cost of more than $300 billion. They include the Air Force F-22 "stealth" jet, the military's Joint Strike Fighter and the Navy's advanced FA-18E/F.

Lockheed Martin Corp. and Boeing Co. are competing to build up to 3,000 Joint Strike Fighters for more than $170 billion in the next century. Variations of the jet would go to the Air Force, Navy, Marines and British Royal Navy.
Lockheed Martin is also developing the F-22. The Air Force wants to buy about 400 of the jets in the next century at a currently estimated cost of $67 billion.
The FA-18E/F, built by McDonnell Douglas Corp. is already undergoing flight testing and the Navy wants to buy 1,000 of them by 2015 at a cost of about $80 billion.
